prompt: Put these hooks in the order the bench logged them when `Life` was created.

choices.text: Every hook from `constructor` to `ngAfterViewChecked`, all over again
choices.why: The component was not created again; only the per-check hooks ran.

choices.text: `ngOnChanges`, `ngDoCheck` and the two `...Checked` hooks
choices.why: Right. The `Init` hooks run once.

choices.text: Only `ngOnChanges`
choices.why: The check that followed also ran `ngDoCheck` and the two `...Checked` hooks.

choices.text: `ngOnInit`, because an input changed
choices.why: `ngOnInit` runs once, after the first `ngOnChanges`.

prompt: Why does the lesson warn about code in `ngDoCheck` and the `...Checked` hooks?

choices.text: They run before the component's inputs are set
choices.why: They run on every check, inputs set or not.

choices.text: They were removed from Angular in version 21
choices.why: They exist and ran on the bench.

choices.text: They run on every check, whatever its cause
choices.why: Right. In a zone.js default component, after every event anywhere.

choices.text: They cannot read signals, so they go stale
choices.why: They can; the concern is how often they run.

prompt: Match each hook with the moment it marks.

pairs.right: an input was set or changed
once, after the inputs were first set
once, after the component's own template was drawn
once, when the component is removed

prompt: Reading a required signal input in the constructor stopped the build with which error?

choices.text: `NG0950`, at run time
choices.why: That is the run-time error lesson 8's test met; here the compiler caught it first.
Right. The compiler saw a required input read where it cannot have a value yet.

choices.text: `TS2551`, a misspelt name
choices.why: The name was right; the timing was wrong.

choices.text: `NG0100`, a value changing between checks
choices.why: That is lesson 7's error, about checks, not construction.

prompt: Why does a `computed` that reads an input work even when it is declared as a field?

choices.text: It reads nothing until someone reads it
choices.why: Right. By then the input is set.

choices.text: Fields are initialised after `ngOnInit`
choices.why: Fields are initialised during construction, before any hook.

choices.text: Angular delays every field until the inputs are set
choices.why: Only the computed's own work is delayed, because it is lazy.

choices.text: A computed copies the input's default value
choices.why: It reads the input when asked; it copies nothing.

prompt: Which of these is still a fair reason to write `ngOnInit` in new code?

choices.text: To read an input into a field once, for the template
choices.why: A `computed` does that and stays in step with the input.

choices.text: To call `inject()`
choices.why: `inject()` belongs in field initialisers or the constructor.

choices.text: A one-off act that needs the inputs
choices.why: Right. An effect would repeat it whenever the input changed.

choices.text: To clean up a timer
choices.why: Cleaning up is `DestroyRef`'s job.

prompt: An old component has `@Input() minutes = 0`, a field `hours`, and `ngOnChanges` that sets `hours`. What replaces the hook and the field with signal inputs?

choices.text: An `effect` that sets an `hours` signal
choices.why: That is the copy-into-a-signal mistake lesson 6 warned about.

choices.text: `hours = computed(() => this.minutes() / 60)`
choices.why: Right. It follows the input with nothing to keep in step.

choices.text: `ngOnInit`, which runs when the input changes
choices.why: `ngOnInit` runs once.

choices.text: A `@let` in the template
choices.why: The class would lose the value, and the question is about the class.

choices.text: Only the new values, without the old ones
choices.why: It receives each change's previous and current value.

choices.text: Nothing at all; the hook reads the inputs itself
choices.why: It receives a `SimpleChanges` object.

choices.text: A `SimpleChanges`, one entry per changed input
choices.why: Right. With `previousValue`, `currentValue` and `firstChange`.

choices.text: The whole component, before and after
choices.why: It receives the inputs that changed, not the component.

prompt: After `Remove`, the clock without `DestroyRef` kept logging `tick`. Why?

choices.text: The `@if` hides components rather than destroying them
choices.why: `@if` destroyed it; `ngOnDestroy` would have run.

choices.text: Angular never knew about the interval
choices.why: Right. It was started with a browser API, so stopping it was the component's job.

choices.text: Signals keep their component alive
choices.why: The interval did, by holding a reference to it.

choices.text: `look` reloaded the page
choices.why: The page stayed loaded; the leak is inside it.

prompt: Which of these does the planner need to clean up by hand when a component goes?

choices.text: A `resource` request still running when it goes
choices.why: A resource ends with its component on its own.

choices.text: An `effect`, created in the constructor
choices.why: Effects stop with the component that created them.

choices.text: A listener added with `window.addEventListener`
choices.why: Right. A browser API, so the component stops it.

choices.text: A `computed` that reads the session list
choices.why: A computed holds no resource that outlives it.

prompt: Inside a component, `inject(___).onDestroy(...)` registers what to run when the component is destroyed.
In the constructor, `document.querySelector('app-bench p')` found nothing. In `afterNextRender`, the paragraph was 18 pixels tall. What changed in between?

choices.text: The browser loaded the stylesheet
choices.why: The paragraph did not exist at all in the constructor, styled or not.

choices.text: Angular drew the template into the DOM
choices.why: Right. `afterNextRender` runs after that write.

choices.text: The `viewChild` query found the paragraph
choices.why: The query found it because it now existed, which is the real change.

choices.text: The component was checked twice in development mode
choices.why: The second check changes nothing in the DOM.

prompt: Why should reading `offsetHeight` not be done in a `computed` or a template?

choices.text: `offsetHeight` is not available in Angular
choices.why: It is a DOM property, available once the element exists.

choices.text: Computed signals cannot return numbers
choices.why: They return anything.

choices.text: It forces a layout during a check
choices.why: Right. Layout belongs after rendering, which is what `afterNextRender` is for.

choices.text: It runs only on the server
choices.why: It runs only in the browser.

prompt: In which situation does lesson 23 make `afterNextRender` matter more?

choices.text: When the page has no stylesheet loaded yet
choices.why: Styles are not the issue; the server is.

choices.text: When the page is first drawn on a server
choices.why: Right. There is no layout or focus there, and it runs only in the browser.

choices.text: When every component in the tree is OnPush
choices.why: OnPush does not change when rendering happens.

choices.text: When tests run in jsdom
choices.why: Lesson 23 is about server-side rendering, not tests.

prompt: Match each job with the tool the lesson recommends for new code.

pairs.left: focus an element once it is drawn

prompt: How many lifecycle hooks does the planner have at the end of this lesson?
An old component subscribes to a timer in `ngOnInit` and unsubscribes in `ngOnDestroy`, forty lines apart. What does the lesson suggest instead?

choices.text: Moving both into `ngAfterViewInit`
choices.why: The view is not involved, and the distance remains.

choices.text: Letting the timer run, since Angular stops it
choices.why: Angular does not know about timers started with browser APIs.

choices.text: Start it in the constructor and register its stop with `DestroyRef` beside it
choices.why: Right. Setup and cleanup in one place.

choices.text: An `effect` that restarts it on every change
choices.why: The timer has no signal to follow; an effect adds nothing.
